title: The sandals on the throne
hook: Bharata refuses the throne and rules under Rama's sandals; why Hindus bow at the feet
carry: touching feet means: you lead, i serve

segments.voice: Yesterday: shoka, grief, and an arrow in the dark that came home. Karma ripens, even decades later. And the one person all this was for hasn't even heard yet.

Bharata has been away the whole time, at his grandfather's kingdom, far to the west. Messengers tell him only: come home, quickly. He rides for days with a bad feeling. Ayodhya is silent. No music, no crowds. In her rooms, his mother Kaikeyi greets him with the news as if it were a gift. Your father is dead. Rama is in the forest. The kingdom is yours. I did it for you. She's waiting to be thanked. Everything she did, the wishes, the exile, a husband's death, was for this moment.
screen: `BHARATA RIDES HOME.` → `A SILENT CITY.` → `THE KINGDOM IS YOURS.`

segments.voice: Bharata doesn't thank her. He's horrified. In Valmiki he turns on his mother with fury and grief: you've destroyed this family, and you've made me the reason. He performs his father's funeral rites, then says what he'll do with the throne. Nothing. It isn't mine. He gathers the mothers, the priests, the ministers and an army, and goes into the forest to bring Rama home. Lakshmana sees the army and assumes the worst. He's wrong. Bharata falls at Rama's feet and begs him to come back and be king. And Rama, who loves him, says no. Our father gave his word; I have to keep it for fourteen years. Two brothers argue, each trying to give the other the kingdom. So Bharata asks for one thing: Rama's sandals. He carries them home on his head, sets them on the throne, and rules in Rama's name, a caretaker, not a king. He moves to a village outside the city, dresses like a hermit, and waits fourteen years. Notice what he chose to honor: not Rama's crown. His feet. That's one of the most Hindu gestures there is. Children bend to touch the feet of parents and grandparents, and get a blessing back. Students bow at a teacher's feet. In temples and home shrines, sandals called padukas stand for God or a guru and are honored with flowers. Bowing at someone's feet says: you lead, I serve. Bharata ruled a whole kingdom that way. For many Hindus, he's the Ramayana's quietest hero: devotion that serves instead of owning.
screen: `IT ISN'T MINE.` · `THE SANDALS ON THE THRONE.` · `A CARETAKER, NOT A KING.` · `PADUKAS: HONORING THE FEET.` · then, large: `TOUCHING FEET MEANS: YOU LEAD, I SERVE.`

segments.voice: If there's an elder you love nearby today, you might bend and touch their feet, or simply bow your head to them, and let them bless you. If you pray, bow to an image of God or of a teacher, the way Bharata bowed to two sandals. If not, think of someone whose lead you'd gladly follow, and thank them for one thing.
Paduka, Rama's sandals, placed on the throne Bharata refuses, so he rules as caretaker in Rama's name for fourteen years.
Your line: touching feet means you lead, I serve. Two sandals kept a throne for fourteen years. That's day forty-four.

howItsDone: Many Hindus honor Bharata as the model of selfless devotion; the sandals on the throne are much-loved in Ramlila and temple art. Touching elders' feet for a blessing, and honoring padukas, the sacred sandals of God or a guru, are everyday Hindu practices.
